claim: At a September 16, 1975 Church Committee hearing, CIA Director William Colby displayed a device resembling a .45-caliber pistol that silently fired a small dart. The hearing record described the system as a nondiscernible microbioinoculator for clandestine inoculation and said it was designed to resist detection in a later examination. The committee was investigating the CIA's unauthorized retention of shellfish toxin after President Richard Nixon's 1969 order to destroy biological-agent stocks.

sources.label: U.S. Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities (Church Committee), hearing transcript, September 16, 1975 — “Unauthorized Storage of Toxic Agents”
sources.quote: a dart device for clandestine and imperceptible inoculation with BW/CW agents

sources.label: Maryland Today (Univ. of Maryland) — “Keeping an Eye on the Spies”
sources.quote: designed to fire a dart of frozen shellfish toxins for use in undetectable assassinations

sources.label: Military.com — “The CIA's 'Heart Attack Gun': A Cold War Weapon for Targeted Assassinations”
Haley Press / @strategichaley, Instagram reel DVOtv6QCTFf (Feb 26, 2026) — surfacing source

notes: The published Church Committee transcript identifies the displayed pistol, silent small dart, nondiscernible microbioinoculator program, detection-resistant design, and retained shellfish toxin. The popular 'heart attack gun' label is not used in the claim. The surfacing reel uses the weapon in a fictional confession; the record is limited to the documented device and hearing.
